note: The gate registry — the enumeration against which gate coverage is
measured (manifest item 4, specs/SPEC.md, the lifetime discriminator; kogaki#16).
An unregistered gate is the uncovered-by-default shape, so this file
is what makes a coverage claim mean anything: the number the check
prints is a fraction OF this list and of nothing else.
Deliberately NOT checks/registry.json, and the argument is mechanical
before it is philosophical: every entry there names a `file` that must
exist under checks/, and check-registry-conformance.sh fails any entry
that does not (checks/check-registry-conformance.sh:21-27). A gate is
not a file in checks/, so a gate row is a dangling entry by
construction. The admission record is check-loop economics too — tier,
runtime_ms, removal_signal — and a gate has no runtime and no loop
position. Merging would mean fabricating those fields or making them
optional, and an optional admission field is exactly the gap kogaki#6
was filed to close. Same coverage discipline, different admission
economics, so two artifacts.
Home: src/gate-registry.json, beside src/gate-schema.json — the schema this
file satisfies. It is a runtime-read carrier (src/terrain.mjs loads it at
module start), which is the criterion kogaki#765 used to site such carriers
in flat src/.

gate_call_bound_note: THE DECLARED BYTE BOUND ON A COMPOSED GATE CALL (kogaki#1090).
It is read by `composeGateCall` in the executor and is measured over the
EXACT bytes `emitGateDeclaration` would write to `<gate>.gate-call.json` --
`JSON.stringify(tool_input, null, 2)` plus its trailing newline -- because that
file is what `.claude/hooks/advance-terrain.py` relays and what the PreToolUse
equality check compares against. A bound measured over anything else would
bound a string nobody delivers.
WHY A BOUND EXISTS AT ALL. The call reaches the session on a PostToolUse
hook's `additionalContext` (kogaki#1081), and the open-gate interval
(kogaki#1028) refuses `Read` while the gate is open -- so a payload the
channel truncates cannot be fetched from inside the session, a reconstructed
one is refused by the equality check as designed, and the run wedges with the
gate unrendered. That is the 2026-09-11 live run (`gate-unrendered`), whose
ID call was 42,432 bytes.
WHERE 8192 COMES FROM, measured rather than argued. On the harness these runs
execute in, a 16,015-byte tool payload was delivered whole and a 61,440-byte
one was spilled to a file behind a 2 KB preview; the wedging call at 42,432
was in the spilled class, and the last ID call delivered whole (2026-09-10)
was 646. 8192 sits below every observed spill and above the largest
legitimate composed call measured -- the `agents` tag's 61-row bounded
listing, whose whole call is about 5 KB. Moving it is a measurement and not a
preference: state the new observation beside the new number.
ONE BOUND FOR EVERY GATE, not one per row of `gates`. The constraint belongs
to the DELIVERY CHANNEL, which is the same for every gate this runtime
raises, so a per-gate bound would be eight declarations of one fact and seven
chances to declare it wrong.
THE REFUSAL IS LOUD AND PRE-GATE. Over the bound `emitGateDeclaration` writes
NOTHING -- no declaration, no `gate-call.json`, no open-gate pointer -- and
the executor exits non-zero, so the refusal reaches the session on the channel
kogaki#1085 opened. It is deliberately NOT the `gate_call_unavailable` arm,
which writes a pointer and leaves the gate renderable from the declaration: an
oversized payload has no smaller rendering for a session to fall back to, and
inviting one would be the model-composed payload kogaki#1028 removed.

gates.question: Which tag does the survey open on?

options.label: Use a method other than co-tags — no other method exists yet, and this option is routed nowhere

gates.dynamic_options: THE LARGEST SERVED TAGS, up to three, ids equal to the tag names (kogaki#1029, revising the 2026-09-04 shape on kogaki#856). The one-standing-option shape was refused by the harness's selector at the first live hook-driven run on 2026-09-09: the selector renders two to four options and nothing under two, so the gate never appeared. The format is the surface's and the values are the run's: `src/terrain.mjs` ranks this run's survey sections by Lesson count and offers the top three as options, each id the tag name so a click lands exactly where a typed tag lands; the standing option rides beside them as the premise negation the gate owes; any other tag is free text. The declaration's `tag_listing` key still holds the runtime's own pre-selection listing byte-for-byte, rendered above the question.

unrouted_options.other-method: No method other than co-tags exists yet, so this option is routed NOWHERE (owner ruling 1, 2026-09-04). The executor records the capture — the answer is evidence and the gate carrier owes the row — and then REFUSES the advance, naming the option, leaving the wait outstanding so the gate can be re-rendered. Routed nowhere is not the same as accepted: without this the option id lands where a tag name goes and the run dies two states later in `compose_input`, telling the owner that "other-method" is not in the survey's vocabulary — a refusal that misdescribes what they did. One of exactly two ways to answer deserves a refusal that names it (PR #898 round 1).

gates.question: Which groups do you want to read in full?

options.label: None of these — nothing is read in full, and the grouping stands

gates.dynamic_options: NONE, and that is this gate's shape rather than an omission. The owner supplies a G/SG id LIST, and a list is not an option: a composed run routinely carries more groups than the selector affordance's four, and any per-group option set would either truncate the view or refuse the run outright. So exactly two ways to answer exist — the standing negation, or free-form entry of the id list — which is the shape `terrain-tag-selection` already has in this same registry and for the same reason. What the run DOES carry is not an option: the declaration's `groups_listing` key holds a BOUNDED PROJECTION of the runtime's own composed grouping — one line per Group and per SubGroup, carrying the id, the Lesson count and the name and nothing else — and `composeGateCall` puts it inside the question text above the question line, so the reading the owner answers over is part of the payload the PreToolUse equality check admits and a listing that arrives missing, paraphrased or reordered is a byte difference rather than a regret. IT CARRIED THE WHOLE `reports/CoTagGroups.md` RENDERING UNTIL kogaki#1090, and that is where the bound comes from: for the `agents` tag the whole rendering is 40,789 characters, the composed call was 42,432 bytes, the delivery channel truncated it, and the live run of 2026-09-11 wedged with this gate unrendered. The claims, the coherence lines, the disclosures and the member id lists stay in the artifact, which the listing's own header names as the full reading — a pointer BESIDE a reading rather than instead of one, which is the distinction kogaki#1087 turned on. The projection is read off that artifact's heading lines rather than recomputed from the survey, so it cannot say anything the file the owner is pointed at does not; a heading it cannot reduce is a refusal and never a dropped row. IT WAS A POINTER (`groups_artifact`, kogaki#890) UNTIL kogaki#1087: naming the artifact left the rendering to a session that might or might not open it, and on the live run of 2026-09-10 the owner was asked which groups to enter with the grouping nowhere on screen. The wording changed in the same act — "enter" and "composed groups" are executor vocabulary, and this gate is the ONE place the owner's selection now happens, kogaki#1087 having deleted the Strand-selection gate that asked a second time for a token nothing read. REGISTERED AT kogaki#890, AND THE GAP IS THE FINDING RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT: `ID_SELECTION` was this workflow's ONE wait that declared no gate, so its owner input arrived as a bare `--input` the model composed — the channel the 2026-09-04 ruling refuses, surviving in the one state a gate-coverage number computed over the declared gates could not see. The standing negation is the PREMISE NEGATION the gate owes: the wait is reached on the premise that the composed grouping is what the survey should enter, and a gate whose every answer shares a machine-computed premise makes it unfalsifiable at the one moment a human is present to falsify it — a free-text escape is not sufficient, because it is the option a hurried operator skips. consulted: product-lab@7e1bba09ae982ffa7e322463fdb052379c77a77d LESSONS.md:198 fork:false deliberately, and for the same reason as the other terrain gates: the runtime attaches no recommendation to which groups are worth entering, and a ranked recommendation here would be the machine narrowing the survey twice — once by composing the grouping and again by scoring it.

unrouted_options.enter-no-groups: Routed to a REFUSAL, not to a state. The executor records the capture — the answer is evidence and the gate carrier owes the row — and then refuses the advance, naming the option and leaving the wait outstanding so the gate can be re-rendered once the grouping changes. Routed nowhere is not the same as accepted: without this the option id would land where a G/SG id list goes and the run would die two states later in `full_report`, telling the owner that "enter-no-groups" is not a known id — a refusal that misdescribes what they did.

options.label: The settled set is what should change — go back through Terrain and re-settle; no Brief is started and nothing is written (a Brief never fetches)

gates.dynamic_options: The 2-3 options are composed per run FROM THE SETTLED STRAND SET ONLY (the read-not-invented rule; ids thesis-1..thesis-3), each in plain register with its round-trip concession stated (normative home: specs/spec-brief-draft-design/DESIGN.md, plain register and the round trip, kogaki#752; the round-trip INSTRUCTION itself is operational text in src/packet-template.md, kogaki#749, so a composer reads the template and this row cites the ground rather than the text. The pre-split home was the deleted SPEC-style-contract's own plain-register clause; that spec was DELETED at kogaki#749 and its pinned served quote was carried into the design record with it). EACH OPTION IS A (THESIS, SLUG) PAIR (v11, kogaki#518, owner ruling 2026-08-17 recorded in kogaki#494's thread): `enter` derives one slug per candidate from that candidate's own Thesis and carries it in the option, and adopting an option adopts both halves — the mint consumes the adopted pair. There is no second slug question anywhere in this flow; the retired brief-slug-approval gate is gone from this registry rather than left unraised, because two gates whose owner_decision resolves to the same vocabulary entry at the same artifact are ONE gate, the second being a defect. THE PAIR RIDES ONE GATE ONLY UNDER THE TWO CONDITIONS the durable home and the entry point, v11, BINDS IT BY, and both are declared here rather than left to the runtime. SEPARATELY RENDERED: the slug is its own visible, NAMED element of the option LABEL — `<Thesis rendering, concession included> — Brief: <bare slug>`, carrying the BARE slug and never a theses/ path. The site moved from the option BODY at kogaki#567, under the release condition the durable home and the entry point, v11, attached to the body placement when it declared it try-one-first; WHAT THAT CONDITION NOW STANDS AT is read from kogaki#567 and from the durable home and the entry point, never asserted here — a gate record names its carrier and does not assert that carrier's state (consulted: product-lab@541e5958 LESSONS.md:97). THE PROPERTY IS UNCHANGED and only its site moved: the name is set off and named rather than folded into the Thesis prose, which is what stops a second decision class being ratified unseen. The body entry is REMOVED rather than left beside the label — two sites for one value is what a half-finished move leaves behind, and the check refuses it. SEPARATELY DECLINABLE: an owner who adopts a listed Thesis but wants a different name says so in the SAME one answer — `adopt --thesis <id> --slug <name>` — which costs neither a restatement of the Thesis nor the abandonment of the option; the runtime's lowercase-and-hyphens refusal covers a malformed one. The run's full declaration is written into the machine-local run state beside the composed candidates (pre-Thesis state is machine-local, the durable home and the entry point, v9) — the same run-workspace siting as the terrain gates. The standing negation option is standing because the composing premise — this settled set supports a Thesis — is the machine's, and its negation routes back through Terrain, never a Brief fetch. fork:false deliberately: the runtime attaches no recommendation among its own candidates — ranking them would be the machine adopting a Thesis by another name, and the Thesis is the first piece of substantive OWNER judgment in the flow. The free-text answer becomes the adopted Thesis verbatim, with its name derived from it, and does not discharge the negation option.

The standing negation option is the PREMISE NEGATION the gate owes: every option is generated on the premise that the adopted Thesis and the settled Strand set support a composed structure, and its negation routes to a refusal that writes nothing rather than to a state. fork:false deliberately, and for the sharper of the two available reasons: the Candidates differ in READER EXPERIENCE, which is the owner's own judgment about the article they are writing, so a recommendation here would be the runtime choosing the reader's journey by another route.

unrouted_options.none-of-these: Routed to a REFUSAL, not to a state. The executor records the capture — the answer is evidence and the gate carrier owes the row — and `adopt-candidate` then refuses, naming the answer, leaving the Brief's sequence unwritten and every Candidate adoptable again once the Thesis or the settled set changes. Recording the decline rather than discarding it is what makes a re-raised gate legible: the capture carries both answers in order and `validateOwnerAnswer` reads the LAST, so an owner who declines and later selects has a record of having changed their mind rather than a silent overwrite.
